description: Hi everyone! We are Team Champion Maker, a passionate, dynamic, and creative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 local event in Hanoi.
summary:
ICE FLOW is an intelligent maritime safety and risk-management system designed for commercial vessels navigating cold, ice-filled waters. As climate change accelerates Arctic ice fracturing, smaller fragmented icebergs pose a severe, hidden threat to ships that conventional radars often miss.

To address this, we developed ICE FLOW—a proactive navigation assistant that combines Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from NASA’s NISAR and ESA’s Sentinel-1 with real-time crowdsourced captain reports. The platform features smart risk-aware routing (functioning like 'Google Maps for the ocean') and triggers near real-time red alerts when hazardous drifting ice enters a vessel's safety buffer. ICE FLOW is critical because it empowers small and mid-sized commercial fleets to safely unlock shorter polar shipping lanes, minimizing collision risks, saving fuel, and protecting crews against unprecedented climate hazards.
details:
1. What does the ICE FLOW project do and how does it work? When we first started exploring ocean and sea ice topics using NASA data, our team asked ourselves: "How can ships navigating the Arctic or Antarctic oceans know where submerged ice is ahead of time to avoid it, especially under thick cloud cover?" Driven by that question, we built ICE FLOW — an intelligent maritime navigation mapping system designed to help vessels avoid colliding with drifting ice.

The system works by fetching open satellite data from NASA (including real-time iceberg data from NASA EONET, cloud-penetrating radar imagery from Sentinel-1 / NISAR via ASF DAAC, and glacier boundaries from NSIDC). After automatically converting the coordinates to standard world map projections and calculating the dangerous submerged ice keel beneath the water's surface, the A* pathfinding algorithm automatically plots a safe detour route, while allowing users to simulate real-time voyages on both a 2D map and a 3D globe.

2. Benefits and real-world impact of the project

  • Protecting crew safety: Helps captains detect both massive icebergs and smaller ice fragments through dense cloud cover early on, minimizing the risk of tragic collisions like the Titanic disaster in the past.
  • Saving fuel and time: Instead of taking overly wide detours out of caution, ships can closely follow safe boundaries (an 18-nautical-mile buffer zone) thanks to continuously updated satellite data.
  • Raising awareness about climate change: Helps people visualize the rate of ice melt and the movement of massive ice sheets at Earth's two poles.

3. Tools, programming languages, and software used As 11th-grade students working with large-scale space data for the first time, we chose lightweight, accessible, yet powerful web technologies:

  • Programming languages: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3 (combined with Tailwind CSS for UI design).
  • Backend & Data processing: Node.js and Express.js to build a middleware server that calls NASA APIs, extracts .kmz file packages, and converts polar projection coordinates into standard latitude and longitude.
  • Graphics & Mapping: Leaflet.js library for the 2D navigation map and Three.js / WebGL to render an intuitive 3D globe model.
  • Development tools: Visual Studio, Git, and GitHub for team source code management.

4. Creativity and key factors considered by the team

  • Solving the "blind spot" problem between satellite passes: We realized satellites do not capture the same spot continuously, and ice is always drifting. Therefore, our team incorporated a physics formula (ocean currents combined with 2.5% of wind velocity) to forecast ice drift direction over the next 24 hours, while assigning a Confidence Level label (High / Medium / Low) based on satellite capture latency so captains do not become complacent with outdated data.
  • Relatable, human-centered simulation experience: Instead of just displaying dry numbers, we designed a feature that simulates a real ship moving across the 2D/3D map, automatically sounding a red alert siren when approaching ice, highlighting danger zones with specific advice for sailors, and presenting a heartfelt certificate of honor upon arriving safely at port.
  • Additional factors considered: The team placed special emphasis on stability under weak network conditions (allowing direct uploads of .kml, .csv, and .geojson files downloaded locally from NASA) and hard-locking the continental coastlines of the Arctic and Antarctic so the algorithm never mistakenly routes a ship onto landfast ice shelves.
